The compound was isolated from plants in the genus Strychnos, where it has long been known for its toxic properties. Historic records suggest its use in Europe as early as 1640 to kill animals and humans.

card.title: Tetrodotoxin linked to zombieism in Haiti
card.body: Tetrodotoxin has been alleged to cause zombieism and is said to have been used in Haitian Vodou preparations by a sorcerer called the bokor. This idea first appeared in Zora Neale Hurston's 1938 book Tell My Horse and was later popularized by Wade Davis's 1985 book and Wes Craven's 1988 film, both titled The Serpent and the Rainbow.

card.title: In pufferfish and beyond
card.body: Tetrodotoxin is found mainly in the liver and gonads of pufferfish, globefish, and toadfish, as well as in blue-ringed octopuses, rough-skinned newts, and moon snails. It can also be present in some shellfish and is produced by bacteria like Pseudoalteromonas, Pseudomonas, and Vibrio through symbiotic relationships. Human exposure occurs when consuming improperly prepared fish organs.

card.title: From discarded by-product to a 'wonder drug'
card.body: In 1952, Chemical Industry Basel synthesized thalidomide but discarded it because it had no effect on animals. In 1957, Chemie Grünenthal acquired it and Heinrich Mückter led the discovery program. While preparing reagents, Mückter's assistant Wilhelm Kunz isolated a by-product recognized by pharmacologist Herbert Keller as an analog of glutethimide.

Once widely sold for morning sickness, it was removed from the market in 1961 after causing severe birth defects in over 10,000 possibly 20,000 infants.

card.title: From Mesoamerica to Germany
card.body: Native Mesoamerican peoples, such as the Totonacs of modern-day Veracruz, Mexico, discovered and cultivated vanilla as a flavoring for beverages by the early 15th century. The Aztecs used vanilla in chocolate drinks called xocohotl. In 1874, Ferdinand Tiemann and Wilhelm Haarmann deduced vanillin's structure and developed a synthesis from coniferin, starting industrial production in Holzminden, Germany.
